stem: What uniquely identifies a time series in Prometheus?

options.text: Its metric name plus its full set of label key-value pairs
options.note: Right. Name plus labels together form the series identity.
Many series share a metric name. The labels tell them apart.

options.text: The target it was scraped from
options.note: The target contributes job and instance labels, but the identity is name plus all labels.

options.text: The timestamp of its first sample
options.note: Timestamps belong to samples, not to the series identity.

explanation: Every time series is uniquely identified by its metric name and optional key-value pairs called labels.

sources.title: Data model › Metric names and labels

stem: How many distinct time series are shown here?

options.note: Right. The first and last lines have identical names and labels (label order doesn't matter), so they're the same series.
Look closely: two lines have the same name and the same label set, just written in a different order.
The GET line and the /users line both differ from the others in at least one label value.
They share a metric name, but different label values mean different series.

explanation: A series is its name plus its set of labels. Label order in the notation doesn't matter, so `{method="POST", handler="/messages"}` and `{handler="/messages", method="POST"}` are the same series.
hint: Compare the label sets, not the line order or text.

sources.title: Data model › Metric names and labels

stem: What does a single sample consist of?

options.text: A float64 (or native histogram) value and a millisecond-precision timestamp
options.note: Right. That's the definition in the data model docs.

options.text: A metric name and a list of labels
options.note: That's the series identity. A sample is a value and a timestamp within a series.

options.text: A string message and a severity
options.note: That sounds like a log line. Prometheus samples are numeric.

options.text: An integer value and a second-precision timestamp
options.note: Values are float64 (or native histograms) and timestamps have millisecond precision.

explanation: Samples form the actual time series data. Each is a float64 or native histogram value plus a millisecond-precision timestamp.

stem: Which selector refers to the same series as http_requests_total{job="api"}?

options.note: Right. The metric name is stored internally as the special label `__name__`.
The internal label is `__name__`, with double underscores. `name` would be an ordinary user label.
There's no special label called `metric`.
Labels go in curly braces, not square brackets.

explanation: Metric names are internally represented as a label pair with the special label name `__name__`.
hint: Reserved internal labels start with two underscores.

stem: Label names beginning with which prefix are reserved for internal Prometheus use?

options.note: Right. Names starting with `__` are reserved for Prometheus internals.
A single leading underscore is allowed. The reserved prefix is two underscores.
There's no such reserved prefix.
Colons are reserved in metric names for recording rules, but that's a different rule.

explanation: Label names beginning with `__` (two underscores) must be reserved for internal Prometheus use.

sources.title: Data model › Metric names and labels

stem: Why shouldn't exporters or directly instrumented code use colons in metric names?

options.text: Colons are reserved for user-defined recording rules
options.note: Right. The data model reserves colons for recording rule names.
Colons are perfectly valid characters. They're reserved by convention.

options.text: Colons separate the metric name from its value
options.note: A space separates the name and labels from the value in the text format.

options.text: Colons mark a metric as a counter
options.note: Counters are marked by type metadata, and by convention a `_total` suffix.

explanation: The data model notes that colons are reserved for user-defined recording rules and should not be used by exporters or direct instrumentation.
hint: Which kind of rule creates new series with structured names?

sources.title: Data model › Metric names and labels

stem: How does Prometheus treat a label whose value is the empty string?

options.text: As if the label does not exist
options.note: Right. An empty label value is equivalent to the label being absent.

options.text: As a distinct value that creates a separate series
options.note: The docs say empty values are equivalent to the label not existing.

options.text: As an error that fails the scrape
options.note: Empty label values don't fail the scrape.
No such conversion happens.

explanation: Labels with an empty label value are considered equivalent to labels that don't exist.
hint: An empty tag is no tag.

sources.title: Data model › Metric names and labels

stem: Which labels does Prometheus attach automatically to series it scrapes from a target? Select all that apply.

options.note: Right. The configured job name the target belongs to.
Right. The host:port of the scraped target.
There's no automatic `env` label. You'd add one yourself through configuration or relabeling.
Every series has a metric name, but `__name__` isn't attached by the scrape to identify the target. `job` and `instance` are the automatic target labels.

explanation: When scraping, Prometheus attaches `job` (the configured job name) and `instance` (the host:port that was scraped) to identify the target.
hint: One identifies the group, the other identifies the specific endpoint.

stem: In Prometheus terms, what is an instance?

options.text: An endpoint you can scrape, usually corresponding to a single process
options.note: Right. Several instances with the same purpose form a job.

options.text: A whole group of replicated processes
options.note: That's a job. An instance is one member of it.
A sample is a value plus timestamp. An instance is a scrape endpoint.
The term refers to a scrape target endpoint, not the server.

explanation: An endpoint you can scrape is called an instance, usually corresponding to a single process. A collection of instances with the same purpose is a job.
hint: Think of one replica among several.

stem: Which of these are poor choices for label values because of cardinality? Select all that apply.

options.note: Right. User IDs are unbounded, so each one would create new series.
Right. Email addresses are unbounded, and the docs call them out explicitly.
A small, bounded set of values makes a good label.
Status codes are a small, bounded set, which suits a label well.

explanation: Every unique label combination is a new time series. Don't use labels for high-cardinality dimensions such as user IDs, email addresses or other unbounded sets.
hint: Which values could grow without limit as you gain users?

stem: What does the instrumentation guide suggest about label cardinality?

options.text: Keep most metrics below about 10, and investigate alternatives for anything over 100
options.note: Right. Most metrics should have no labels at all, and above 100 you should rethink the design.

options.text: Cardinality doesn't matter because Prometheus compresses everything
options.note: Each label set costs RAM, CPU, disk and network, so cardinality matters a lot.

options.text: Aim for at least 1,000 label values to get fine-grained data
options.note: That's the opposite of the guidance.

options.text: Always add a unique request ID label for traceability
options.note: Request IDs are unbounded, which is exactly what to avoid. That's a job for logs or tracing.

explanation: The guide suggests keeping cardinality below 10 for most metrics, limiting the exceptions, and looking for alternative solutions if a metric has or could reach cardinality over 100.
hint: The numbers in the guide are small.
